title: The Surprising Pleasures of Aging Gracefully
text:
“I hope I die before I get old,” a 21-year-old Roger Daltrey famously sneered on the Who’s 1965 single “My Generation.” At the time, the countercultural upshot was clear: Music was a young man’s game, especially rock and roll. Rock music embodied rebellion and fearlessness. It was about spitting in the face of elders who disapproved of what they could never understand. Who could trust a rock star still playing those kinds of songs well into middle age?

 Of course, the surviving members of the Who are now in their 80s and still performing, despite promises of retirement, because the benefits of playing decades-old songs to adoring crowds remain strong. The expectation of releasing new music has faded away. Audiences come to bask in memories from their youth or share their passions with their kids. The money is excellent. Classic rockers such as the Who, the Rolling Stones, and the Eagles set the template for hugely profitable late-in-life reunion tours; successive generations of bands have followed suit. Now the cycle continues with two defining British bands from the mid-’90s, who have reunited to remind the public that the music from the Britpop era was really just that good.

 Two new documentaries about Oasis and Pulp, inspired by their respective circa-2025 tours, capture the spirit of the bands while digging into how they’ve processed the passage of time—to fascinating effect. Oasis was the most successful of the Britpop groups; led by the brothers Noel and Liam Gallagher, its swaggering rock music conveyed the maximalist melodrama of being young and in love with women, drugs, and ambition. Pulp was arguably the coolest Britpop group, whose front man, Jarvis Cocker, led with a sly, eccentric style and literary sensibility that stood in sharp contrast to his noisier peers. Like the Gallaghers, he seemed to genuinely relish his celebrity, but his relatively reserved personality made his indulgences seem chic and deliberate—potential grist for the lyrical mill, not simply rock-and-roll decadence.

 Don’t Look Back in Anger chronicles the highly anticipated Oasis reunion tour in 2025 that rejuvenated the band’s public image, following an acrimonious 2009 split. What Do You Do for an Encore? , for its part, combines a traditional concert film with a snapshot survey of Pulp’s lengthy career, and is narrated with wry humor by Cocker himself. Both documentaries attempt to bridge the gap between nostalgia for a past heyday and sanguine acceptance of a hazy future, while asking a simple yet difficult question: How do rock and rollers grow old without embarrassing themselves?

 In the ’90s, the British music media spent a lot of time publicizing an astroturfed competition between Oasis and its fellow chart-topper Blur , its baroque, Anglophilic-pop counterpart. Amid this sniping, Pulp stood apart as the round peg in a sea of square holes. A working-class kid from Sheffield, Cocker was 31 when Pulp’s best-known single, “Common People,” climbed the U.K. charts in 1995, making him something of an elder statesman relative to his musical peers. Draped in dapper outfits accentuating his lanky frame, Cocker represented an androgynous, cerebral alternative to the era’s boisterous masculinity.

 What Do You Do for an Encore? sketches out how Cocker graduated from a teenage outsider to a patron saint for sensitive, horny misfits. The documentary is anchored by performances from Pulp’s sold-out shows at London’s O2 Arena in June 2025 and is interspersed with “commercial breaks” during which Cocker, in voice-over, cheekily breaks the fourth wall to narrate his early childhood and experiences with fame. The film highlights Cocker’s alt-lothario stage presence as he sings about a world of hedonism and heartbreak, coming off as a veteran actor who’s only grown deeper into his role.

 In contrast, Don’t Look Back in Anger ’s directors, Will Lovelace and Dylan Southern, frequently cut away from Oasis’s performances to focus on the crowd itself, singling out individuals in tears or mid-embrace. They also incorporate numerous testimonials about how Oasis affected fans’ lives. Some are compact voice-over explanations about the power of friendship or self-confidence. Others are longer on-screen tributes, including one from a South Korean haenyeo (a female diver responsible for harvesting sea life) who explains how Oasis’s music gave her the strength to plunge into the water. Another features a survivor of the 2017 Manchester Arena bombing, who discusses how the song that gives the documentary its name helped her process survivor’s guilt.

 The film also goes to some lengths to imply that the Gallaghers’ reunion mended the culture at large, or at least provided the world with sufficient escapism and hope. Early in the film, Liam says, “When Oasis split up, things just went shit,” which is followed by a montage of news footage that includes the January 6 riots, Donald Trump dancing at a MAGA rally, and a food-delivery robot getting hit by a car. (No montage of positive world events following the tour is to be found.) Later, a Manchester priest speaks to a sparsely attended congregation about how crowds of Oasis fans resemble a pilgrimage and indicate a “shared longing for healing.” The message is clear: No matter what else has happened, the world is better with Oasis in it.

 Patience for this level of hyperbole obviously depends on the viewer’s affection for Oasis. As a longtime listener, I often found myself chafing against some of the overwrought fan reactions, despite their transparent sincerity. But I can attest to the accuracy of how the film portrays the public fervor that the Oasis reunion inspired in the U.K. In the days leading up to the Dublin show, my friends and I could not walk a few feet in the city without seeing an Oasis T-shirt or bucket hat. The show itself was pandemonium, with approximately 80,000 people singing along to every word of every song. I rarely attend concerts that are on this scale and get this level of hype, so at times I simply watched the crowd move in almost otherworldly unison. “I’d never come across an atmosphere like that at a concert before,” remarked Cocker, who attended one of Oasis’s Wembley shows. “It was like being at some kind of religious rally or something. It was amazing.”

 Oasis has been the subject of other documentaries, but my favorite is 2016’s Supersonic . The film is laser-focused on the Gallagher brothers’ conversational interplay, which, by default, makes it one of the funniest music documentaries ever released. Hearing Noel and Liam trade barbs about the other’s professional acumen or recount the same drug-fueled period in radically different terms, you might think that their real talent was giving hilarious interviews that exemplified their vulgar charisma.

 This time around, Noel and Liam—who have recently reconciled amidst years of estrangement—don’t exchange insults. Rather, the film chronicles their growing appreciation for each other as the tour transpires, which is expressed in hand-holding and hugs onstage. “It was all forgiven without saying a word,” Noel says of their beef, a notable reversal. They are older, softer men, who routinely express their gratitude for the opportunity to play 30-year-old songs to sold-out stadiums.

 This makes emotional sense for the Gallaghers and the film, but the scant display of their comedic chops is a little disappointing. Ironically, Don’t Look Back in Anger comes most alive whenever Noel and Liam speak semi-extemporaneously about each other. At one point, Noel expounds in voice-over about Liam’s aloof appeal before saying, as if he is remembering in real time, “I forgot how funny he was.” Cut to Liam, wearing enormous glasses, profanely explaining why he stands still onstage and then pondering whether Mick Jagger secretly wishes he didn’t have to do “‘Jumpin’ Jack Flash’ nonsense.” Noel cracking up at this rant in the background pulls more heartstrings than any onstage embrace.

 Pulp has also been the subject of a prior documentary: 2014’s A Film About Life, Death & Supermarkets , which depicts what was at the time billed as the group’s final U.K. show, in 2012, in Cocker’s hometown of Sheffield. Like Supersonic , this earlier film explains the appeal of Pulp better than the new one. Yet the 2026 documentary captures the emotions that come with unexpected longevity. In Supermarkets , for example, Cocker mentions wanting to provide Pulp with the tidy ending it didn’t get during its initial run. In Encore , however, he expresses the humility that comes with being unable to predict the future, now that his band has reunited. “You might be forgiven for thinking, after all these years, Why do we keep going? ” he narrates in his baritone. “I think the question you should really be asking yourself is this: Why wouldn’t we?”

 The Gallagher brothers arrive at a similar conclusion, as Liam expresses a quasi-mystical disbelief at the capacity of Oasis’s music to bring people together: “It’s bigger than me and Noel. It doesn’t belong to us.” Unlike Pulp, which is now on hiatus, Oasis will gear up for another worldwide tour next year, certainly to chase the hundreds of millions of dollars the band made in 2025, but also possibly to search for an answer to how and why, per Liam, “Oasis saves.” For my money, trying to determine the mass appeal of Oasis is like trying to understand why so many people like beer; you either get it or you don’t. But the choruses are really catchy.

 Despite some frustrations, watching Don’t Look Back in Anger and What Do You Do for an Encore? in quick succession proved strangely gratifying. I was aware that the filmmakers used my built-in affection for both of these bands to sell an image of them as wiser, more prudent men. Yet it is wise to appreciate your audience, and your remaining ability to galvanize them with your music. These films suggest that second or third acts are never guaranteed in life, especially in the realm of pop stardom. The Gallaghers and Cocker have composed many songs that are now old enough to drink and drive, and each carries power far beyond their initial impact. Performing onstage, these documentaries show, is a reminder that these older men are vessels for community and significance. At the same time, the hits don’t exist without them. The vessels themselves are worthy of celebration.
